guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
How This Relates to IFS

Internal Family Systems, or IFS, overlaps with this guide. It recognizes protective parts and teaches people to approach them without shame or combat. The “meet the protector first” sequence is compatible with IFS.

My reparenting method diverges from IFS at an important point. Standard IFS treats the healer as the Self, a calm and compassionate inner source assumed to be available once parts “unblend.” I emphasize the inner adult you build and practice occupying: Nurturer, Protector, and Leader, Guide, or Guru.

The borrowed-adulthood phase sharpens the difference. When the calm inner source cannot be reached, the person can borrow one adult function from a relationship, image, plan, or action and gradually internalize it.

I have no use for another neo-Advaita, spiritual-bypassing claim that a perfect Higher Self is already waiting underneath everything. A trustworthy adult function is built through care, boundaries, action, and direction.

IFS calls these wounded young parts “exiles.” I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition.

IFS “unburdening,” often done after witnessing a part’s origin story, can be powerful. It can also become dramatic, memory-focused, suggestive, or destabilizing—especially for people prone to dissociation, DID-like fragmentation, or spiritual bypass.

The expanding map of managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, and new subparts can also become a maze. Some practitioners use the model gently. Others seem to deepen identity fragmentation while trying to resolve it. Institutionalization doesn’t automatically make a framework clearer, safer, or more true.

A skilled, grounded, non-suggestive, trauma-informed IFS therapist may help, especially when they understand dissociation. For inner-child pain, shame, attachment wounds, self-abandonment, or the absence of a reliable inner adult, a good reparenting therapist may fit better. Understand both the strengths and pitfalls before choosing.

(The guide's link: "spiritual-bypassing" goes to http://goenka.u-dont-exist.com/ .)

brief:
- the main points, in the guide's order: (1) IFS overlaps with this method: it recognizes protective parts and teaches people to approach them without shame or combat, and "meet the protector first" fits with it. (2) His method diverges from IFS at an important point: standard IFS treats the healer as the Self, a calm and compassionate inner source assumed to be available once parts "unblend"; he emphasizes the inner adult you build and practice being (the Nurturer, the Protector and the Guide; the guide also calls the third the Leader or Guru). (3) Borrowed adulthood sharpens the difference: when that calm inner source can't be reached, you can borrow one adult job from a relationship, an image, a plan or an action and take it in gradually. (4) His first-person line, kept as he published it (with its link on "spiritual-bypassing"): "I have no use for another neo-Advaita, spiritual-bypassing claim that a perfect Higher Self is already waiting underneath everything." A trustworthy adult is built through care, boundaries, action and direction. [The settled paragraph: exiles, and unburdening.] (5) The expanding IFS map (managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts) can become a maze; some practitioners use the model gently, others seem to deepen fragmentation while trying to resolve it; institutionalization doesn't automatically make a framework clearer, safer or truer. (6) A skilled, grounded, non-suggestive, trauma-informed IFS therapist may help, especially one who understands dissociation; for inner-child pain, shame, attachment wounds, self-abandonment or the absence of a reliable inner adult, a good reparenting therapist may fit better; understand the strengths and pitfalls of both before choosing.
- already in the article, so said briefly or pointed back to: "That's one grown-up doing three jobs, not three more people moving in" (The Chicken-and-Egg Problem); borrowed adulthood is a whole h1 (Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult); Borrow Hindsight says "No perfect Higher Self is handing down answers."
- his first-person lines are his story, kept as close to his published wording as reads naturally: "My reparenting method diverges from IFS at an important point.", "I emphasize the inner adult you build and practice occupying".
